pages.description: Most dengue infections cause mild flu-like symptoms or no symptoms at all. But at least one person has died from this year’s outbreak in Florida, where health experts worry the disease will become more common in the future
pages.text: Florida Is Facing Its Worst Dengue Outbreak in Decades, With at Least 524 Locally Acquired Cases. Here's What to Know Skip to main content Dengue is a viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes. Joao Paulo Burini via Getty Images This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue , a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009 , according to Forbes ’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025. Most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness . But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the New York Times ’ Anemona Hartocollis. Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue. “It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris , an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times . “This is so very much of an eye-opener.” Here’s what to know about dengue. What is dengue? Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , which are both present in Florida , among other places. pages.text: FLSA Protections to Pump at Work | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content FLSA Protections to Pump at Work Revised January 2026 Coverage for certain employees of rail carriers and motorcoach services operators begins December 29, 2025. Employees may be exempt if an employer demonstrates that compliance would require significant expense or results in unsafe conditions. The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) requires employers to provide reasonable break time for an employee to express breast milk for her nursing child for one year after the child's birth each time such employee has need to express the milk. Employees are entitled to a place to pump at work, other than a bathroom, that is shielded from view and free from intrusion from coworkers and the public. What You Should Know Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA): Most nursing workers are entitled to reasonable break time and a private space to pump at work for up to one year after their child’s birth. Most employers are required to provide covered employees with space that is functional for pumping milk, shielded from view, free from intrusion, available as needed and not a bathroom. Learn more about Employer Responsibilities . New Law Expanding Pumping at Work Protections On December 29, 2022, the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 became law. Food Poisoning Symptoms Nov. 24, 2025 Key points Symptoms of food poisoning depend on the type of germ you swallowed. The most common symptoms include diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Severe food poisoning can cause bloody diarrhea, diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days, fever over 102°F, frequent vomiting, and dehydration. Symptoms You can get sick with food poisoning after swallowing certain germs, like Salmonella or E. coli . Your symptoms may vary, depending on the germ you swallowed. Symptoms can range from mild to serious and can last for a few hours or several days. Some germs can make you sick within a few hours after you swallow them. Others may take a few days to make you sick. The most common symptoms of food poisoning are: Diarrhea Stomach pain or cramps Nausea Vomiting Fever If you have diarrhea or vomiting, be sure to drink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration (not having enough water in your body). Food Safety Basics Mar. 9, 2026 At a glance Food can sometimes contain harmful germs, such as Salmonella and norovirus, that can make you sick. If you eat food containing germs, you can get a foodborne illness (sometimes called food poisoning). Some foods are more likely to contain germs, including raw flour and dough, raw chicken, and raw milk. "Food safety" refers to steps you and others can take to prevent foodborne illness. Overview Foods can sometimes be contaminated with germs that can make you sick. Some examples include Salmonella, norovirus, and Campylobacter. What is food safety? Food safety refers to practices that can reduce your risk of getting food poisoning. This is a significant public health burden that is largely preventable. The FDA Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) is transforming the nation’s food safety system by shifting the focus from responding to foodborne illness to preventing it. Congress enacted FSMA in response to dramatic changes in the global food system and in our understanding of foodborne illness and its consequences, including the realization that preventable foodborne illness is both a significant public health problem and a threat to the economic well-being of the food system. FDA has finalized several rules to implement FSMA, recognizing that ensuring the safety of the food supply is a shared responsibility among many different points in the global supply chain for both human and animal food. The FSMA rules are designed to make clear specific actions that must be taken at each of these points to prevent contamination. pages.text: For a New Perspective on Luxor's West Bank, Hop on a Bike | National Geographic TRAVEL For a New Perspective on Luxor's West Bank, Hop on a Bike One of the world’s great open-air museums, Luxor’s West Bank is also a living, breathing neighbourhood best explored by bicycle. The Colossi of Memnon can easily be seen from the saddle on biking tours. Claire Thomas By Zoey Goto Published September 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). A coach rumbles past and, for a fleeting moment, I feel a pang of envy for the air-conditioned cocoon its passengers are almost certainly enjoying. Then I look around. From behind tinted windows, they’re missing the street theatre playing out around us. “Cycling is the best way to really see Luxor,” Sayed Setouhy calls over his shoulder, his crown of cropped black curls silhouetted against the sun. “You have the freedom to stop, take pictures and discover things that people in cars and coaches don’t.” It’s morning in Luxor and the city on the banks of the Nile is limbering up for the day. Gaggles of schoolchildren in matching uniforms chat at the roadside as a donkey cart clip-clops past. Laundry flaps from balconies, while dogs lie sprawled in scraps of shade, untroubled by the day’s gathering pace. I’m on Luxor’s West Bank, a stretch of farmland, village streets and ancient monuments that’s perfect for exploring on two wheels. pages.text: For Over Four Years, the Hirshhorn Worked to Revitalize Its Sculpture Garden. Today, It's Home to a 'King and Queen,' a 'Wish Tree' and a 55,000-Pound Vertical Swimming Pool Artwork Skip to main content King and Queen , Henry Moore, bronze, 1952-1953 Rick Coulby / Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden We descend underground into a cavernous space, seeing our own distorted reflections in stainless-steel panels on the walls. Designed by Hiroshi Sugimoto , even this entryway to the newly renovated Hirshhorn Sculpture Garden is a work of art. “You’ll notice that the distortion kind of changes levels,” says the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden ’s acting head curator Marina Isgro . “It’s sort of at adult-height here, and then as you walk in, it kind of becomes child-height. Sugimoto is really welcoming visitors of all sizes to play with their reflections here in this space.” As we continue the journey into the sunken garden, we find ourselves in a play of light and shadows and stone and bronze, among flowers, trees and the occasional insect. A reflecting pool and a platform for stage performances sit in the middle of the grounds. pages.text: For the Gwich'in People, the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge Isn't a Political Issue, It's Home Skip to main content Science | December 2021 For the Gwich’in People, the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge Isn’t a Political Issue, It’s Home Journey to the far north of Alaska, where the Indigenous communities hunt caribou, the backbone of the region’s ecosystem Jeffrey Peter, of Old Crow, Yukon, cleans a caribou hide during an autumn hunt. When camping, the hide is used as a mattress; at home, it’s clothing. Peter Mather Jeffrey Peter, of Old Crow, Yukon, cleans a caribou hide during an autumn hunt. When camping, the hide is used as a mattress; at home, it’s clothing. Peter Mather In the Gwich'in language, there’s a name for the area just north of the Brooks Range, the mountains that run along the northern rim of Alaska and divide the densely forested interior from the spare Arctic coast. Where the land flattens out into low-lying tundra before meeting the Beaufort Sea is Iizhik Gwats’an Gwandaii Goodlit , or “the sacred place where life begins.” The name honors the role this 1.5-million-acre swath of Arctic coastal plain plays as the primary calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou, a herd of more than 200,000 animals. This crucial habitat is where tens of thousands of pregnant cows migrate each year to give birth. Porcupine caribou, named for a river within their range, can trek 3,000 miles in a year to reach their calving grounds north of the Brooks Range. SCIENCE LAELAPS For the Love of Dinosaurs By Riley Black Published May 26, 2013 • 10 min read Last month, Scientific American/FSG Books was kind enough to publish my ode to dinosaurs and the science that is changing our perceptions of how they lived – My Beloved Brontosaurus . I wrote the following op-ed to accompany the book’s release, published here after failing to find a niche elsewhere. I was a little dinomaniac. I can’t recall exactly when the fever set in, but I ceaselessly pestered my parents to tape every movie and television show even remotely associated with the word “dinosaur”, my curiosity further fueled by museum trips, toys, and lavishly-illustrated books. I’ve still got the bug. Even now, I feel the same compulsion to chew on scattered dinosauriana, in both their scientific and pop culture garbs. But why? The inexorable pull of dinosaurs is a mystery. When I talk about dinosaurs to anyone who isn’t quite so enamored as I am, but remembers their own dinosaur phase or is suffering through that of their own children, they often ask why dinosaurs have such a persistent hold on pop culture and our imagination. Dinosaurs are seemingly everywhere, from lunchboxes and sports mascots to bleeding-edge scientific discoveries. Premium HISTORY & CULTURE Face of 9,000-Year-Old Teenager Reconstructed The meticulous process, based on a skull from a Greek cave, reveals how our facial features have changed over the millennia. By Sarah Gibbens Published January 20, 2018 • 4 min read Her name is Avgi, and the last time anyone saw her face was nearly 9,000 years ago. When she lived in Greece, at the end of the Mesolithic period around 7000 B.C., the region was transitioning from a society of hunter gatherers to one that began cultivating its own food. In English, Avgi translates to Dawn—a name archaeologists chose because she lived during what's considered the dawn of civilization. Little is known about how she lived and died, but now archaeologists can see the ancient woman's prominent cheekbones, heavy brow, and dimpled chin. Facial features have "smoothed out" over millennia, and humans look less masculine today, says reconstructor Oscar Nilsson. Photograph by Oscar Nilsson Avgi's face was revealed by University of Athens researchers at an event at the Acropolis Museum on Friday. To reconstruct her face was no small feat. FORGE The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Geothermal Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy (FORGE) initiative is a dedicated field site in Milford, Utah, where scientists and engineers can develop, test, and accelerate breakthroughs in enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) technologies and techniques. Led by the University of Utah – Energy & Geoscience Institute (EGI) in association with multiple partner organizations , the Utah FORGE project area is rural, covering less than five square miles, and is situated near the town of Milford in Beaver County, Utah’s Renewable Energy Corridor . This part of the Milford Valley hosts a wind farm, solar photovoltaic plant, a geothermal plant, and several hog farms from which biogas is harvested. pages.title: Former death row prisoners call Byron Donalds to halt future Florida executions | Florida | The Guardian
pages.description: Donalds is governor-elect in state that leads the US in the number of executions, with its 20th this year taking place next week
pages.text: Former death row prisoners call Byron Donalds to halt future Florida executions | Florida | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Florida governor-elect Byron Donalds speaks during Nasa's Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center, in Merritt Island, Florida on 6 November. Photograph: Joe Skipper/Reuters View image in fullscreen Florida governor-elect Byron Donalds speaks during Nasa's Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center, in Merritt Island, Florida on 6 November. Photograph: Joe Skipper/Reuters Florida Former death row prisoners call Byron Donalds to halt future Florida executions Donalds is governor-elect in state that leads the US in the number of executions, with its 20th this year taking place next week Richard Luscombe in Miami Thu 12 Nov 2026 13.58 EST Last modified on Thu 12 Nov 2026 14.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three exonerated former death row prisoners in Florida have called on incoming governor Byron Donalds to halt the state’s record run of executions and review the cases of all 235 prisoners who are now condemned. At a press conference in Tallahassee on Thursday hosted by the advocacy group Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty (FADP), the men said they were seeking a roundtable discussion with Donalds, a Republican, as well as the state’s new legislative leaders in pursuit of a moratorium. Florida leads the country in both executions and exonerations, and next Thursday’s scheduled execution of convicted murderer Thomas Overton will be the state’s 20th this year, one more than the record of 19 set in 2025.
